item.title: The independence still waiting to be completed. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B

On the morning of July 31, in a hotel in Dhaka, the United States Special Envoy for South and Central Asia met India's high commissioner to Bangladesh. The conversation lasted about 90 minutes and took place the day before the envoy called on Bangladesh's prime minister, and that evening the Indian envoy flew to Delhi for consultations. Neither side described what was discussed. Nothing improper occurred. Diplomats meet, and it is the business of every state to advance its own interests. India was pursuing India's. Washington was pursuing America's. Beijing continues to pursue its own across the region. States behave like states, and there is nothing in that to resent. What stayed with me was simpler, and quieter. A consequential conversation about this region took place on Bangladeshi soil, and Bangladesh was not part of it -- and few in Dhaka seemed to think this worth remarking upon. Consider, too, the arrangement itself. The American envoy holds two appointments simultaneously: Ambassador to India, and Special Envoy for South and Central Asia. Delhi recognizes the first and has been visibly uneasy about the second; when he announced in June that he looked forward to working closely with India's incoming envoy in Dhaka, a former Indian foreign secretary objected publicly, observing that American ambassadors to India do not customarily approach Indian envoys posted to third countries. The doctrine has been clear for our country, as recently stated by our foreign minister: Bangladesh would never strengthen ties with one country at another's expense, and seeks good relations with all while advancing its own interests. It is the right doctrine, and I believe it is sincerely held. The question is whether we have built anything capable of carrying it. There is reason for doubt, and it does not require any accusation to see. In February, Bangladesh signed a trade agreement with the United States that lowered our tariff to 19% -- a real and welcome gain for an economy under strain. But the agreement also carried conditions that made it harder for Dhaka to move closer to certain other countries, China foremost among them. Four months later, in Beijing, China proposed the Bangladesh-China-Myanmar Economic Corridor: Road and rail from Yunnan through Myanmar to Chittagong and Mongla. Our foreign minister said, correctly and carefully, that Bangladesh was examining the proposal and had taken no position. Read those two facts together. In February we accepted relief on the condition that our future alignments be constrained. In June we were offered something that tests exactly that constraint. And in July, envoys of two other powers sat in a Dhaka hotel and discussed the region for 90 minutes without us. This is what the loss of strategic autonomy actually looks like. Not occupation. Not humiliation. A sequence of individually reasonable decisions, each defensible on its own terms, which together narrow the range of choices available to the country later. Why do we keep arriving here? I do not believe it is chiefly the fault of foreign capitals, and I do not think it is a failing of the present government alone. It is older than that. Across five decades, our politics has repeatedly sought abroad the confidence it could not settle at home. Where authority rests on a mandate that is contested rather than trusted, where institutions are staffed by loyalty rather than merit, where the press must weigh its words, a government's standing does not rest securely on the consent of its own citizens. It has to be supplemented. And the supplement is always foreign -- Delhi in one decade, Washington in another, Beijing in a third. It is paid for in policy. That is the mechanism, and it explains why strategic autonomy is not, in the first place, a question of foreign policy at all. A government confident of its standing at home does not need to be reassured of its standing abroad, and cannot be moved by the withdrawal of that reassurance. We have rarely sustained such confidence for long. Until we do, our negotiating position will keep being set somewhere other than Dhaka. Nor can a country negotiate freely if it cannot discuss its own affairs freely. The most telling feature of that week was the quiet around it -- the ordinary questions a confident nation asks aloud, unasked. Into that silence rushed rumour: Within a day, versions of events were circulating that the record does not support. When careful reporting recedes, the public appetite to know does not. It merely goes unfed. I have lived in Sweden long enough to be careful about what I claim for it. Swedish foreign policy is not unconstrained. In 2024 Sweden abandoned two centuries of non-alignment and joined NATO -- not in tranquillity, but because Russia had made the older position untenable. Geography pressed on Stockholm as it presses on Dhaka, and Stockholm yielded to it. The difference is not that Sweden escaped constraints. It is that the decision was argued in the Riksdag (parliament), reported by a press nobody had to be brave to read, and afterwards owned by Swedes as their own. No foreign envoy settled it in a hotel room, and no citizen was left to guess what had been agreed on his behalf. That is the whole of what I am asking. Not the freedom to do as we wish -- no country has that. The capacity to make a constrained choice in our own name, in the open, and to answer for it afterwards. That does not require Sweden's wealth. It requires institutions we could build at our present income. Two proposals, then. They are modest, and they can be refused. I write from Stockholm, and I should be honest about what that distance means. I am a Swedish citizen. I will very likely never see Bangladesh again. But my mother is there, and I was born there, and a man does not choose which soil made him. Watching that week gave me no pride. I have looked for a gentler way to say it and not found one. I do not ask that Bangladesh be admired. I ask that Bangladesh not be bullied -- by anyone. We won our political independence in 1971 at a cost this generation cannot fully imagine. But independence was never the achievement of a single morning. It is renewed, or quietly given away, in the ordinary decisions of ordinary years -- in what we sign, in what we ask, in what we permit to be discussed about us in rooms we are not invited into. Bangladesh's future will not be settled in Washington, Delhi, or Beijing. It will be settled in Dhaka, or it will not be settled at all. That is the independence still waiting to be completed. Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s latest remarks -- stressing the efficient use of existing resources and a decisive shift toward energy diversity -- comes at a critical time for our nation, and must be heeded. To say that Bangladesh is navigating an increasingly difficult energy landscape would be an understatement, with recent gas shortages across the nation only the latest example. To that end, the message from the PM should be clear: Our country must diversify, modernize, and use what it already has with far greater discipline. While the Matarbari power plant, which is where the PM delivered his remarks, is not without its share of criticism - which are legitimate given the eventual need to shift away from fossil fuel-generated energy sources - what is also true is that for addressing our immediate energy needs, its efficient operation is critical. Bangladesh must embrace true energy diversity, and for the short run, that does, unfortunately, include fossil fuels as well. However, the transition to renewable sources must be more than rhetoric; the present BNP government has ambitious goals regarding renewable energy, but we will not be close to those goals without action. The PM’s emphasis on using existing resources efficiently also points to a long‑standing problem: Poor maintenance, system losses, and mismanagement. Before adding new megaprojects, which had become the norm, Bangladesh must fix the basics -- reduce transmission losses, upgrade aging lines, and ensure that every kilowatt generated is actually delivered. Energy is not just a sector but the backbone of economic stability. Without reliable power, industries falter, investment slows, and public frustration grows. The responsibility now lies with policy-makers and institutions to act with urgency, discipline, and foresight. Bangladesh must move beyond short‑term fixes and commit to a diversified, efficient, and resilient energy future.

item.title: Coal dominates Bangladesh’s top imports, clinker at second position
item.description:
Around 5,700 categories of goods are imported into Bangladesh each year. The list includes industrial raw materials, fuel, consumer goods and various materials used in development projects.

However, imports of only a handful of these thousands of products account for a huge volume. Some products are imported in quantities exceeding tens of millions of tonnes a year.

An analysis of data from the National Board of Revenue (NBR) and its field offices shows that a total of 158.6 million tonnes of goods were imported through the country’s 46 customs stations in the recently concluded 2025–26 financial year.

The top 10 products accounted for 99.8 million tonnes. In other words, nearly 63kg of every 100kg of imported goods came from these 10 products.

Industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction dominate the top 10. Among food grains, only wheat made the list.

LNG: 13-year import deal secured with one US firm

Clinker loses top spot after 25 years

According to NBR data, clinker—the main raw material used to make cement—was the country’s largest imported product by volume for 25 consecutive years, from the 2000–01 to 2024–25 financial year. That long-standing dominance has now come to an end.

Coal displaced clinker to become the country’s largest imported product in the 2025–26 financial year. Bangladesh imported 20.7 million tonnes of coal during the year.

Several raw materials, including slag, limestone and fly ash, are used alongside clinker in cement production. All four feature among the top 10 imported products.

The rise in coal imports is not unexpected. Demand for coal has increased rapidly for power generation since coal-fired power plants began operating in the country. Six coal-fired power plants accounted for around 75 per cent of total coal imports last financial year.

As a result, coal, once used mainly as fuel and a raw material in industrial factories, has now become the country’s largest imported product by volume.

Clinker second, slag fourth

Clinker, a raw material used in cement production, has dropped to second place after losing its long-held position at the top. The country imported 19.2 million tonnes of clinker in the last financial year.

Several raw materials, including slag, limestone and fly ash, are used alongside clinker in cement production. All four feature among the top 10 imported products. After clinker, another cement raw material, slag, ranks fourth. The country imported 8.3 million tonnes of slag in the last financial year.

Limestone, which ranks sixth, accounted for nearly 6 million tonnes of imports. And, Fly ash, or ash, ranks 10th, with imports of around 5 million tonnes.

Wheat is the only consumer product among the top 10 imported goods. By volume, it ranks fifth. Bangladesh imported 7.434 million tonnes of wheat in the last financial year.

In total, nearly 38.5 million tonnes of the four types of cement raw materials were imported. In other words, cement industry raw materials account for a substantial share of the total volume of the top 10 imported products.

Crushed stone ranks third

Crushed stone ranks third by import volume. Bangladesh imported 16.8 million tonnes of crushed stone in the last financial year. The stone is used in the construction of roads, buildings and various other infrastructure projects.

Alongside crushed stone, large quantities of boulder stone are also imported. The country imported 5.5 million tonnes of boulder stone in 2025-26 financial year, placing it eighth by volume. Boulder stone is used in river management and various development projects.

Wheat the only consumer product in top 10

Wheat is the only consumer product among the top 10 imported goods. By volume, it ranks fifth. Bangladesh imported 7.434 million tonnes of wheat in the last financial year.

Approximately 15 per cent of the country’s demand for wheat is met by domestic production. The remaining 85 per cent or so is met through imports. As a result, wheat is the country’s largest imported food grain by volume.

Amirul Haque, president, Chattogram ChamberMost of the products imported in the largest volumes are industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction. Five of them are raw materials for the cement and steel sectors. Demand for these products will increase as economic activity and investment grow.

Scrap, the raw material for rebar, ranks seventh

Scrap metal, or old iron and iron pieces, the main raw material used to make rebar, ranks seventh. Bangladesh imported around 5.7 million tonnes of scrap in the last financial year. The country’s steel mills melt the scrap to produce billets, which are then used to manufacture rebar and other steel products.

LNG ranks ninth

Liquefied natural gas (LNG), imported to meet fuel demand, ranks ninth. The country imported around 5.1 million tonnes of LNG in the last financial year.

Bangladesh has been importing LNG for several years to make up for shortages in domestic gas supplies. Imported LNG is converted back into gas and supplied to the national grid.

Overall, the top 10 imported products are dominated by fuels such as coal and LNG, raw materials for the cement and steel industries, and materials used in infrastructure construction. Wheat is the only food product on the list.

This means that, by volume, a large share of Bangladesh’s imports is not directly intended for consumption but is used for power generation, industrial production and infrastructure development.

Asked for his views, Amirul Haque, an entrepreneur in the cement and consumer goods sectors and president of the Chattogram Chamber, told Prothom Alo, “Most of the products imported in the largest volumes are industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction.”

“Five of them are raw materials for the cement and steel sectors. Demand for these products will also increase as economic activity and investment grow,” he added.

item.description:
রাশিয়ার তাতারস্তান অঞ্চলের নিঝনেকামস্ক শহরে ইউক্রেনের ড্রোন হামলায় এক শিশুসহ অন্তত ১৩ জন নিহত হয়েছেন। আহত হয়েছেন ৩৯ জন। সোমবার আঞ্চলিক কর্তৃপক্ষ এ তথ্য জানিয়েছে। ব্রিটিশ বার্তা সংস্থা রয়টার্স এ খবর জানিয়েছে।
রাশিয়ার তাতারস্তানের রাজধানী কাজান থেকে প্রায় ২০০ কিলোমিটার দূরে নিঝনেকামস্ক শহরটি মস্কো থেকে প্রায় ৮০০ কিলোমিটার পূর্বে অবস্থিত। হামলায় শহরের একটি তেল শোধনাগারও লক্ষ্যবস্তু হয়েছে বলে জানিয়েছে ইউক্রেনের সামরিক বাহিনী।
রাশিয়ার কর্মকর্তারা জানিয়েছেন, হামলায় বেসামরিক স্থাপনাও ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হয়েছে। তাতারস্তানের আঞ্চলিক প্রধান রুস্তাম মিনিখানভ হামলাটিকে ‘বর্বর’ বলে উল্লেখ করেছেন।
নিহতদের মধ্যে অন্তত সাতজন উজবেক নাগরিক বলে জানিয়েছে কাজানে উজবেক কনস্যুলেট। রাশিয়ায় উজবেকিস্তানের প্রায় ২০ থেকে ৩০ লাখ নাগরিক কাজ করেন।
নিঝনেকামস্ক রাশিয়ার গুরুত্বপূর্ণ তেল ও শিল্পকেন্দ্রগুলোর একটি। শহরটিতে দেশটির অন্যতম বড় ও আধুনিক তেল শোধনাগার তানেকো অবস্থিত। ইউক্রেনের সামরিক বাহিনী জানিয়েছে, রাতের হামলায় তারা ওই শোধনাগারকে লক্ষ্য করেছিল।
রাশিয়ার প্রতিরক্ষা মন্ত্রণালয় জানিয়েছে, রাতভর ইউক্রেনের ৪৫০টির বেশি ড্রোন শনাক্ত ও প্রতিহত করা হয়েছে। হামলার ঘটনায় রাশিয়া তদন্ত শুরু করেছে। রুশ তদন্ত কমিটি এটিকে ‘সন্ত্রাসী হামলা’ হিসেবে অভিহিত করেছে।
এদিকে ইউক্রেনের পূর্বাঞ্চলীয় খারকিভ অঞ্চলে রুশ বাহিনীর গোলাবর্ষণে অন্তত পাঁচজন নিহত হয়েছেন বলে স্থানীয় কর্মকর্তারা জানিয়েছেন। আঞ্চলিক প্রসিকিউটর অফিস জানিয়েছে, চুগুইভ জেলার একটি গ্রামে এই হামলার ঘটনা ঘটে।
ইউক্রেনের প্রেসিডেন্ট ভলোদিমির জেলেনস্কি জানিয়েছেন, রাশিয়ার তেল শোধনাগারগুলোতে হামলা অব্যাহত থাকবে। তার দাবি, মস্কো যুদ্ধের পরিণতি অনুভব করতে শুরু করেছে।

item.title: বেসরকারি হাসপাতাল-ক্লিনিকের লাইসেন্স নবায়নের মেয়াদ হবে দুই বছর
item.description:
দেশের বেসরকারি হাসপাতাল, ক্লিনিক, ডায়াগনস্টিক সেন্টার, ডেন্টাল ক্লিনিক এবং মেডিক্যাল চেকআপ সেন্টারগুলোর লাইসেন্স প্রদান ও নবায়নের মেয়াদ ১ বছর থেকে বাড়িয়ে ২ বছর করেছে সরকার।
সোমবার (১০ আগস্ট) স্বাস্থ্য অধিদফতরের হাসপাতাল ও ক্লিনিকসমূহের পরিচালক ডা. মো. নুরুল ইসলামের সই করা অফিস আদেশে সিদ্ধান্ত বাস্তবায়নের কথা জানানো হয়।
স্বাস্থ্য ও পরিবার কল্যাণ মন্ত্রণালয়ের স্বাস্থ্য সেবা বিভাগের বেসরকারি স্বাস্থ্য ব্যবস্থাপনা-১ শাখার নির্দেশনার পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে এই সিদ্ধান্ত নেওয়া হয়েছে বলে অফিস আদেশে উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে। নতুন এই নিয়ম ২০২৬-২০২৭ অর্থবছর থেকে কার্যকর হবে।
লাইসেন্স প্রাপ্তি ও নবায়নের ক্ষেত্রে কয়েকটি সুনির্দিষ্ট শর্ত মেনে চলার কথা বলা হয়েছে—
ফি জমাদান: ২ বছরের লাইসেন্স ফি এবং ভ্যাট একসঙ্গে সরকারি কোষাগারে জমা দিয়ে এইচএসএম ওয়েবসাইটের মাধ্যমে আবেদন করতে হবে।
পরিবেশ ছাড়পত্র: নতুন লাইসেন্স গ্রহণের ক্ষেত্রে পরিবেশ অধিদপ্তরের অবস্থানগত ছাড়পত্র বা পরিবেশ ছাড়পত্র আবশ্যিকভাবে নিতে হবে।
নারকোটিক লাইসেন্স: যে সমস্ত প্রতিষ্ঠান নারকোটিক বা মাদকদ্রব্য ব্যবহার করে, নতুন লাইসেন্স পাওয়ার পর তাদের অবশ্যই নারকোটিক লাইসেন্স সংগ্রহ করতে হবে।
নিয়মিত তদারকি: পরিবেশ অধিদফতর ও মাদকদ্রব্য নিয়ন্ত্রণ অধিদফতর নিজ নিজ দফতরের হালনাগাদ লাইসেন্স তদারকি করবে।
এছাড়া অধিদফতরের কর্মকর্তা, বিভাগীয় পরিচালক (স্বাস্থ্য), সিভিল সার্জন এবং উপজেলা স্বাস্থ্য ও পরিবার পরিকল্পনা কর্মকর্তারা নিয়মিত স্বাস্থ্য সেবা প্রতিষ্ঠানগুলো পরিদর্শন করবেন। পরিদর্শনে কোনও অনিয়ম বা ব্যত্যয় পাওয়া গেলে লাইসেন্স স্থগিত বা বাতিল করা হবে। বাসস।
